title: Old Bookshop in Tanjung Pinang
subtitle: Discovering a dust-covered notebook filled with handwritten algorithms from the 1980s.
quote: Old paper smells like time that took its time to pass.
excerpt: In a narrow wooden shophouse in Tanjung Pinang, an unexpected discovery: an engineering logbook from 1984 containing hand-drawn flowcharts and Pascal routines that solved problems we still face today.
body:
Tanjung Pinang moves at the pace of an afternoon tide.

Walking down Lorong Pasar Lama, the wooden stilts of centuries-old shophouses creak over the mudflats. Smells of dried salted fish, cloves, and jasmine incense blend in the sea air.

Tucked between a tailor shop and a dried-herb merchant was an unmarked secondhand bookstore. Books were piled from floor to ceiling in teetering towers: yellowed Malay poetry collections, Dutch maritime almanacs, vintage Chinese martial arts novels, and weathered technical manuals.

The Blue Hardcover

Near the back of the shop, resting beneath a stack of 1970s National Geographics, I spotted a faded blue clothbound notebook. Embossed on the cover in gold foil were the words: Telecommunications Maintenance Log — Riau Sector, 1984.

I opened the yellowed pages. Inside, written in impeccable blue fountain pen cursive, were hand-drawn flowcharts, boolean truth tables, and subroutines written in Turbo Pascal for managing microwave relay stations across the islands.

"Note to self: When the monsoon winds shake the antenna tower on Pulau Batam, add a 50ms buffer to the parity handshake. Machines must have grace when the weather is rough."

I touched the dried ink with my thumb. Forty years ago, an engineer sat in this exact climate, fighting packet loss and network jitter using paper and 64 kilobytes of RAM.

We think our modern challenges are unique. We obsess over cutting-edge frameworks and microsecond latencies. But the core problems—communicating across the sea, keeping packets intact, and building systems that endure the storm—have always been the same. We are just the latest custodians of the flame.
